topics.title: Map skills: grid references and compass points
topics.intro: Ordnance Survey maps use a grid of numbered lines. Remember: along the corridor, then up the stairs.
topics.hook: “Never Eat Shredded Wheat” for the compass; “along the corridor, then up the stairs” for grid references.
topics.teach: Explain how to give a 4-figure grid reference.
topics.talk: On a walk, ask her which direction you’re heading using the 8 compass points.

visual.caption: Never Eat Shredded Wheat: N, E, S, W clockwise. North-east (NE) is halfway between north and east.

topics.title: Map scale and symbols
topics.intro: A map’s scale tells you how much smaller it is than real life. On a 1:25 000 map, 4 cm is 1 km.
topics.hook: On a 1:25 000 map, 4 cm = 1 km; on a 1:50 000 map, 2 cm = 1 km.
topics.talk: Look at an OS map together and find a pub, a school and a church.

head: scale
1 cm on the map is
so 1 km on the map is
visual.caption: Contour lines close together = steep slope; far apart = gentle slope.

topics.title: Rivers: processes and landforms
topics.intro: Rivers carve valleys, carry rocks to the sea and build new land. We’ll follow a river from its source to its mouth.
topics.hook: Source to sea: V-shaped valleys and waterfalls up high, meanders in the middle, floodplains and an estuary near the mouth.
topics.teach: Explain how a meander turns into an ox-bow lake.
topics.talk: Next time you cross a river, ask her which course it might be in: upper, middle or lower.

topics.title: Earth’s structure, earthquakes and volcanoes
topics.intro: The ground beneath us is moving, very slowly. Let’s find out what is inside the Earth and why volcanoes and earthquakes happen where they do.
topics.hook: The Earth is like a peach: thin skin (crust), thick flesh (mantle) and a hard stone in the middle (core).
topics.teach: Explain what happens at a destructive plate boundary.
topics.talk: Ask her why Iceland has so many volcanoes.

topics.title: Climate zones and biomes
topics.intro: Why are there rainforests near the Equator and deserts a little further away? Climate decides which plants and animals live where.
topics.hook: Wet at 0°, dry at 30°: rainforests hug the Equator and hot deserts lie near the tropics.
topics.teach: Explain why tropical rainforests are near the Equator.
topics.talk: Ask her which biome the UK is in.

head: biome
where
what it is like
rows: grassland with wet and dry seasons
mild; trees lose their leaves in winter
very cold, no trees, frozen ground (permafrost)
visual.caption: From the Equator towards the poles.

steps: Emergent: the tallest trees poke out
Canopy: a thick roof of leaves
Forest floor: only about 2% of the sunlight
visual.caption: The layers of a rainforest, from the top down.

topics.title: Population, settlement and development
topics.intro: Where do people live, and why? Why do people move? And how do we measure whether a country is rich or poor?
topics.hook: Settlements grew where life was easier: by water (wet point), at a crossing (bridging point) or somewhere safe (defensive site).
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a push factor and a pull factor.
topics.talk: Ask her why your town grew where it did.

visual.caption: Settlements, smallest first. A city of more than 10 million people is a megacity.

topics.title: The Americas: countries and capitals
topics.hook: Capitals are often not the biggest city: Washington, Ottawa and Brasília, not New York, Toronto and São Paulo.
topics.teach: Name three countries in South America and their capitals.
topics.talk: Ask her the capital of Canada (it isn’t Toronto).

topics.title: Africa: countries and capitals
topics.intro: Africa is a continent of 54 countries, not one country! Let’s learn some of the biggest.
topics.hook: Africa is 54 countries, not one, and Nigeria’s capital is Abuja, not Lagos.
topics.teach: Explain why “Africa is a country” is a mistake.
topics.talk: Ask her the capital of Nigeria (it isn’t Lagos).

topics.title: Asia and Oceania: countries and capitals
topics.hook: Sydney and Melbourne were rivals, so Australia built a brand-new capital between them: Canberra.
topics.teach: Name the capitals of China, India and Japan.
topics.talk: Ask her the capital of Australia (it isn’t Sydney).

items.hook: Along the corridor, then up the stairs: read the eastings first, then the northings.

items.prompt: Put these compass points in order, going clockwise from north.
items.explain: Clockwise: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW. “Never Eat Shredded Wheat” helps with N, E, S, W.
items.hook: “Never Eat Shredded Wheat”: N, E, S, W clockwise. The in-between points join their neighbours: NE, SE, SW, NW.
items.example: The Sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west, so you can use it to find your bearings.

visual.caption: Never Eat Shredded Wheat: N, E, S, W clockwise. North-east (NE) is halfway between north and east.

items.prompt: Which compass point is halfway between north and north-west?
items.explain: With 16 points, the in-between points take the name of the nearest main point first: north-north-west (NNW).
items.hook: Say the nearest main point first: north + north-west makes north-north-west.

items.prompt: When giving a grid reference, which do you read first?
items.explain: Along the corridor (eastings), then up the stairs (northings).
items.hook: You have to walk along the corridor before you can go up the stairs: eastings, then northings.

items.prompt: What are the vertical grid lines, numbered along the bottom of an OS map, called?
items.explain: Eastings increase as you go east. Northings increase as you go north.
items.hook: Eastings count up as you go East; Northings count up as you go North.
1:25 000 means 1 cm on the map is 25 000 cm (250 m) in real life, so 4 cm = 1 km.
items.example: Orange OS Explorer maps are 1:25 000; pink OS Landranger maps are 1:50 000.

items.prompt: What do contour lines on a map join together?
items.explain: Contour lines join points at the same height above sea level. Close together = steep slope.
items.hook: Contours are like the rings left round a bath as it drains: one line for each height.
items.example: On an OS map of Ben Nevis, the contours crowd together on its steep north face.

items.prompt: On a map, contour lines are very close together. What does that tell you?

options.feedback: Flat land has contours far apart, or none at all.
Rivers are shown by blue lines, not contours.

items.explain: Close contours mean the height changes quickly over a short distance: a steep slope.
items.hook: Lines close together: a hill to climb. Lines far apart: an easy walk.
items.example: Stanage Edge, a gritstone cliff in the Peak District, shows up as tightly packed contours on an OS map.

items.prompt: On an Ordnance Survey map, what does “PH” stand for?
items.explain: PH marks a pub. “Sch” is a school.
items.hook: “Pub” is short for “public house”: PH.

items.prompt: A black dot with a number next to it on an OS map is a…
items.explain: A spot height shows the exact height in metres at that point.
items.hook: A spot height is a single spot (dot) with its height in metres beside it.

items.prompt: A blue triangle with a dot in the middle on an OS map marks a…
items.explain: Trig points are concrete pillars on hilltops once used for surveying.
items.example: There are trig points on the summits of Ben Nevis, Yr Wyddfa and Scafell Pike; walkers like to touch them at the top.

items.prompt: Which organisation makes Britain’s official maps?
items.explain: Ordnance Survey (OS) began in 1791, mapping the south coast in case of invasion.
items.hook: “Ordnance” means military supplies: the Army’s Board of Ordnance made the first maps.
items.example: The first OS map, published in 1801, was of Kent.

items.prompt: Where does a river usually flow fastest on average: near its source in the hills, or near its mouth?

options.text: Often near the mouth, where less energy is lost
Always near the source, because it is steepest
options.feedback: Mountain streams look fast because they splash over rocks, but friction slows them. Lower down, rivers are deeper and smoother, so the average speed is often higher.

options.text: Rivers flow at the same speed everywhere

items.explain: This surprises most people! Steep upland streams lose lots of energy to friction. Downstream the channel is wider, deeper and smoother.
items.hook: Smooth is speedy: rocks and shallow water slow mountain streams down with friction.

items.prompt: What is the start of a river called?
items.explain: The source is often a spring or a bog in the hills.
items.hook: Source = Start; Mouth = where it Meets the sea.
items.example: The Thames begins at a stone marking its source in a field near Kemble, Gloucestershire.

items.prompt: Where a river meets the sea is called its…
items.explain: The mouth is where the river ends, at the sea or a lake.
items.hook: Source = Start; Mouth = where it Meets the sea.
items.example: The Thames’s mouth is a wide estuary that meets the North Sea near Southend-on-Sea.

items.prompt: A smaller river that joins a bigger one is called a…
items.explain: Tributaries join the main river at a confluence.
items.hook: A tributary pays tribute: it gives its water to the main river.
items.example: The River Kennet is a tributary of the Thames, joining it at Reading.

items.prompt: The place where two rivers meet is called a…
items.explain: Many towns grew at confluences, such as Pittsburgh, or Koblenz on the Rhine and Moselle.
items.hook: Con = together, fluence = flowing: two rivers flowing together.
items.example: In York, the River Foss flows into the River Ouse.

items.prompt: The area of land drained by a river and its tributaries is called a…
items.explain: The edge of a drainage basin, usually high ground, is the watershed.
items.hook: Like a bathroom basin: all the water inside the rim drains to one plughole.
items.example: Rain falling on Oxford, Reading or London all drains into the Thames basin.

items.prompt: Which type of erosion is the sheer force of water forcing air into cracks in the riverbank?
items.explain: Hydraulic action: the force of water. Abrasion: rocks scraping the bed. Attrition: rocks knocking each other smaller. Solution: dissolving rock.
items.hook: HAAS: Hydraulic action, Abrasion, Attrition, Solution, the four ways rivers erode.
items.example: Like a jet wash blasting a patio, the sheer force of the water does the work.

items.prompt: Which process makes stones smaller and rounder as they knock into each other?
items.explain: That is why stones near a river’s mouth are small and smooth.
items.hook: Attrition: rocks attack each other. Abrasion: rocks attack the bed and banks.
items.example: Stones near a river’s mouth are small and smooth; boulders in mountain streams are big and jagged.

items.prompt: Pebbles bouncing along a river bed are being transported by…
items.explain: Traction: big boulders rolled. Saltation: pebbles bounced. Suspension: fine silt carried in the water. Solution: dissolved minerals.
items.hook: Saltation comes from the Latin for “leap”: pebbles hop. Boulders roll, silt floats, minerals dissolve.

items.prompt: What shape of valley does a river make in its upper course?
items.explain: In the upper course the river cuts downwards, making steep V-shaped valleys with interlocking spurs. (U-shaped valleys are made by glaciers.)
items.hook: V for vertical: rivers cut down into a V. Glaciers gouge out a U.
items.example: Fast mountain streams in the Lake District and Snowdonia have cut steep-sided V-shaped valleys into the hills.

items.prompt: A meander that has been cut off from the river forms…
items.explain: Erosion narrows the neck of a meander until the river cuts through, and deposition seals off the old loop.
items.hook: An ox-bow is the U-shaped collar of an ox’s yoke: a curved loop left behind.
items.example: The Severn winds in great meanders around Shrewsbury; the Mississippi’s floodplain is dotted with ox-bow lakes.

items.prompt: A waterfall forms where a river flows over hard rock lying on top of…
items.explain: The soft rock erodes faster, undercutting the hard rock, which collapses. The waterfall moves upstream, leaving a gorge.
items.hook: Hard on top, soft below: the soft rock is undercut, the hard ledge snaps off and the falls step back.
items.example: High Force on the River Tees pours over hard whinstone sitting on softer limestone and shale.

items.prompt: The flat land beside a river in its lower course, which floods, is called the…
items.explain: Each flood deposits silt, making floodplains very fertile.
items.hook: The floodplain is the plain that floods, and every flood leaves fertile silt behind.
items.example: Tewkesbury, where the Avon meets the Severn, was badly flooded in 2007.

items.prompt: Which river is usually listed as the longest in the world?
items.explain: The Nile, about 6,650 km, is usually listed as the longest. Some scientists measure the Amazon as slightly longer, so the two are close rivals; the Amazon carries far more water than any other river.
items.hook: The Nile is number one for length; the Amazon is number one for water.
items.example: The Blue and White Niles meet at Khartoum, then the Nile flows north through Egypt past the pyramids.

items.prompt: Put these river features in the order you would usually meet them, from source to mouth.
items.explain: Waterfalls in the upper course; meanders in the middle course; ox-bow lakes on the floodplain; the estuary at the mouth.
items.hook: Up high it falls, in the middle it bends, low down it loops and leaves lakes, then it widens to the sea.
items.example: On the Tees: High Force up high, a meander wrapped round Yarm, then the estuary at Middlesbrough.

items.prompt: What is the Earth’s mantle mostly made of?

options.text: A deep sea of liquid lava
options.feedback: A very common idea! The mantle is mostly solid, but hot enough to flow like extremely thick toffee over millions of years.

options.text: Hot water and steam under pressure
options.feedback: The mantle is rock, not water.

items.explain: Magma forms only where rock partly melts, for example where plates move apart or one sinks under another.
items.hook: The mantle is thick toffee, not soup: solid rock that creeps very slowly.

items.prompt: How fast do tectonic plates move?

options.feedback: Much slower than that: centimetres per year.

options.text: They don’t move at all any more
options.feedback: They do move, and GPS can measure it.

items.explain: A few cm a year adds up: over 200 million years the Atlantic Ocean opened up.
items.hook: Plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
items.example: The Atlantic widens by a few centimetres a year, nudging Britain and North America apart.

items.prompt: Put the layers of the Earth in order, from the outside in.
items.explain: Crust, mantle, outer core (liquid), inner core (solid, about 5400°C).
items.hook: Like a peach: skin (crust), flesh (mantle) and a stone (core) in two parts, liquid outside and solid inside.
items.example: Compared with the whole Earth, the crust is about as thin as the skin on an apple.

items.prompt: Which layer of the Earth is solid iron and nickel, as hot as the surface of the Sun?
items.explain: The inner core is solid because the pressure is so great, even though it is around 5400°C.
items.hook: Squeezed so hard it cannot melt: the inner core stays solid even at about 5400°C.

items.prompt: At what kind of plate boundary do plates move APART, letting magma rise?
items.explain: Constructive boundaries make new crust, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge through Iceland.
items.hook: Constructive: constructing new crust as the plates pull apart.
items.example: At Þingvellir in Iceland you can walk in the rift between the North American and Eurasian plates.

items.prompt: At what kind of boundary does an ocean plate sink beneath a continental plate?
items.explain: Destructive boundaries cause violent volcanoes and earthquakes, as in the Andes and Japan.
items.hook: Destructive: the ocean plate is destroyed as it sinks and melts.
items.example: Mount Fuji in Japan and the volcanoes of the Andes sit above destructive boundaries.

items.prompt: At which kind of boundary do plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes but no volcanoes?
items.explain: The San Andreas Fault in California is a conservative boundary.
items.hook: Conservative: crust is conserved, neither made nor destroyed; the plates just slide.
items.example: San Francisco lies beside the San Andreas Fault and was wrecked by an earthquake in 1906.

items.prompt: The point on the Earth’s surface directly above where an earthquake starts is the…
items.explain: The focus is underground, where the rocks slip. The epicentre is the point on the surface above it.
items.hook: Epi means “on top of” in Greek: the epicentre is on top of the focus.

items.prompt: Which instrument measures earthquakes?
items.explain: Seismometers record ground shaking. A barometer measures air pressure; an anemometer measures wind speed.
items.hook: Seismos is Greek for “earthquake”: a seismometer measures the shaking.
items.example: The British Geological Survey records a few hundred earthquakes in the UK each year, mostly too small to feel.

items.prompt: Molten rock underground is called magma. What is it called when it reaches the surface?
items.explain: Magma underground; lava above ground.
items.hook: Magma is in the Middle (underground); Lava has Left the volcano.
items.example: Etna in Sicily and Kīlauea in Hawaii often send out rivers of glowing lava.

items.prompt: What is the name for the zone of volcanoes and earthquakes around the edge of the Pacific Ocean?
items.explain: About three-quarters of the world’s active volcanoes lie around the Pacific.
items.hook: Picture a ring of fire round the Pacific: Japan, Indonesia, New Zealand, the Andes and Alaska.
items.example: Mount St Helens (USA, 1980) and Mount Fuji (Japan) are both on the Ring of Fire.

items.prompt: What was the name of the supercontinent that existed about 300 million years ago?
items.explain: Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had once been joined in Pangaea. Few believed him until the 1960s.
items.hook: Pangaea is Greek for “all lands”: every continent joined into one.
items.example: On a map, the bulge of Brazil fits into the curve of West Africa like a jigsaw piece.

items.prompt: Which Roman town was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79?
items.explain: Ash preserved Pompeii so well that we can still walk its streets.
items.hook: Pompeii was Preserved: ash buried it so fast that it was frozen in time.
items.example: Vesuvius still towers over Naples and is one of the most closely watched volcanoes in the world.

items.prompt: Which of these is the largest desert in the world?

options.feedback: The Sahara is the largest HOT desert. A desert is defined by low rainfall, not heat, and Antarctica gets very little.
The Gobi is large, but smaller than both Antarctica and the Sahara.

items.explain: Deserts get less than about 250 mm of precipitation a year. Antarctica qualifies, and it is huge.
items.hook: A desert is dry, not necessarily hot: Antarctica is the biggest desert of all.

items.prompt: Which biome, near the Equator, is hot and wet all year with the most species on land?
items.explain: Tropical rainforests like the Amazon get over 2000 mm of rain a year and stay hot because the Sun is high all year.
items.hook: Hot and wet every day: near the Equator it rains most afternoons.
items.example: You can walk through an indoor rainforest at the Eden Project in Cornwall; the real giant is the Amazon.

items.prompt: Put the layers of a rainforest in order, from the top down.
items.explain: Emergent trees poke above the canopy; the canopy is a thick roof of leaves; the understorey is dim; the forest floor gets only about 2% of the sunlight.
items.hook: “Every Cheeky Uncle Falls”: Emergent, Canopy, Understorey, Floor. Think eagles, monkeys, jaguars, ants.

steps: Emergent: the tallest trees poke out
Canopy: a thick roof of leaves
Forest floor: only about 2% of the sunlight
visual.caption: The layers of a rainforest, from the top down.

items.prompt: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
items.explain: The Sahara covers much of North Africa, about the size of the USA.
items.hook: Sahara means “desert” in Arabic, so “Sahara Desert” really means “Desert Desert”!
items.example: Saharan dust sometimes blows all the way to the UK and leaves an orange film on cars.

items.prompt: Hot deserts are found about 30° north and south of the Equator. Why?
distractors: they are closest to the Sun
there are no rivers or lakes
items.explain: Air rises at the Equator, drops its rain, then sinks around 30°, warming and drying as it falls.
items.hook: Air rises wet at 0° and sinks dry at 30°.
items.example: The Sahara, the Arabian Desert and the Australian deserts all lie near the tropics.

items.prompt: Which cold, treeless biome near the Arctic has ground frozen all year beneath the surface?
items.explain: The frozen ground in the tundra is called permafrost.
items.hook: Tundra is too cold for trees; permafrost is PERMAnently FROzen ground.
items.example: Reindeer, Arctic foxes and snowy owls live on the tundra of northern Canada, Alaska and Siberia.

items.prompt: Which biome of evergreen conifer forests stretches across Canada, Scandinavia and Russia?
items.explain: The taiga is the largest land biome in the world.
items.hook: Taiga = trees (conifers); tundra = too cold for trees.
items.example: Endless spruce and pine forests across Siberia and Canada are home to moose, wolves and bears.

items.prompt: Which tropical grassland with scattered trees, wet and dry seasons, is home to lions and zebras?
items.explain: Savannas lie between rainforests and deserts, as in East Africa.
items.hook: Picture an African plain: golden grass, flat-topped acacia trees, a wet season and a dry season.
items.example: In the Serengeti, in Tanzania, more than a million wildebeest migrate across the savanna each year.

items.prompt: The UK’s natural biome, before people cleared most of it, is…
items.explain: Deciduous trees like oak and beech lose their leaves in winter.
items.hook: Deciduous comes from the Latin for “falling off”: the leaves drop each autumn.
items.example: Sherwood Forest and the New Forest are survivors of the oak woods that once covered much of Britain.

items.prompt: Which warm ocean current keeps the UK milder than other places as far north?
items.explain: Without it, UK winters would be much colder, more like Canada’s at the same latitude.
items.hook: The North Atlantic Drift is the UK’s central heating.
items.example: Thanks to it, palm-like plants grow in Cornwall and subtropical gardens thrive at Inverewe in north-west Scotland.

items.prompt: From which direction does the UK’s most common (prevailing) wind blow?
items.explain: South-westerly winds bring mild, wet air from the Atlantic, which is why the west of the UK is wetter.
items.hook: South-west winds make the west wet.
items.example: Seathwaite in the Lake District gets over 3 m of rain a year; London gets about 0.6 m.

items.prompt: Put these settlements in order, smallest first.
items.explain: A conurbation is where towns and cities have grown together, like Greater Manchester.
items.hook: “Happy Villagers Take City Coaches”: hamlet, village, town, city, conurbation.
items.example: Greater Manchester is a conurbation: Manchester, Salford, Bolton, Stockport and more grew into one.

visual.caption: Settlements, smallest first. A city of more than 10 million people is a megacity.

items.prompt: A city with more than 10 million people is called a…
items.explain: Tokyo, Delhi and Shanghai are megacities. London has about 9 million people.
items.hook: Mega means “great”: a megacity has more than 10 million people.
items.example: Jakarta, Dhaka and Tokyo are among the world’s biggest megacities, each with over 30 million people: more than three times London.

items.prompt: A settlement that grew up where a river could be crossed has what kind of site?
items.explain: Many towns ending in “-ford” grew at river crossings, such as Oxford.
items.hook: Listen for -ford and -bridge: Oxford, Stamford, Cambridge.
items.example: London grew where the Romans first bridged the Thames.

items.prompt: A settlement built near a reliable water supply such as a spring has a…
items.explain: Before taps, water was vital. A dry point site, on the other hand, avoids flooding.
items.hook: Wet point: near water. Dry point: up out of the floods.
items.example: Villages along the foot of the South Downs grew where springs bubble out of the chalk.

items.prompt: A reason that makes people want to LEAVE a place is called a…
items.explain: Push factors: war, few jobs, drought. Pull factors attract people: jobs, safety, family.
items.hook: Push factors push you out; pull factors pull you in, like a magnet.
items.example: In the 1800s, low farm wages and a lack of work pushed many people out of the countryside and into towns.

items.prompt: The growth in the proportion of people living in towns and cities is called…
items.explain: Over half the world’s people now live in urban areas.
items.hook: Urban comes from the Latin “urbs”, a city.
items.example: In 1800 most people in Britain lived in the countryside; today over 80% live in towns and cities.

items.prompt: Roughly how many people live in the world (2020s)?
items.explain: World population passed 8 billion in November 2022.
items.hook: Counting to 8 billion, one number a second, would take over 250 years.
items.example: That is well over 100 times the UK’s population of nearly 70 million.

items.prompt: Which country has the most people (since 2023)?
items.explain: India overtook China in 2023, with over 1.4 billion people.
items.hook: India overtook China in 2023: more than 1 person in 6 on Earth lives in India.

items.prompt: Which of these is the best single measure of how developed a country is?

options.text: None is perfect: combine several measures
How many tall buildings its capital has
options.feedback: Buildings don’t tell you about most people’s lives.

options.text: How big the country is in area
options.feedback: Size has little to do with development.

items.explain: Measures like GDP per person, life expectancy and literacy are combined in the Human Development Index (HDI).
items.hook: The HDI mixes three things: a long life, a good education and a decent income.
items.example: Iceland, Norway and Switzerland usually top the HDI table; the UK is usually in the top 20.

items.prompt: The average number of years a person in a country can expect to live is called…
items.explain: Life expectancy is around 81 years in the UK.
items.example: Life expectancy is about 81 in the UK, but under 60 in some countries, such as Chad and Nigeria.

items.explain: This is the United States.

items.prompt: What is the capital of the United States?
items.explain: The capital of the United States is Washington, D.C. Not New York!
items.learn: The capital of **the United States** is **Washington, D.C.**. Not New York!
items.hook: D.C. stands for District of Columbia: a special area that belongs to no state.

items.explain: This is Canada.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Canada?
items.explain: The capital of Canada is Ottawa. Ottawa, not Toronto or Vancouver.
items.learn: The capital of **Canada** is **Ottawa**. Ottawa, not Toronto or Vancouver.
items.hook: Queen Victoria picked Ottawa in 1857: it sits on the river between English- and French-speaking Canada.

items.explain: This is Mexico.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Mexico?
items.explain: The capital of Mexico is Mexico City.
This is Brazil.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Brazil?
items.explain: The capital of Brazil is Brasília. Brasília was built as a new capital in 1960.
items.learn: The capital of **Brazil** is **Brasília**. Brasília was built as a new capital in 1960.
items.hook: Brasília was built from scratch in the middle of Brazil, to draw people inland from the coast.

items.explain: This is Argentina.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Argentina?
items.explain: The capital of Argentina is Buenos Aires.
items.hook: Buenos Aires means “good airs”.

items.explain: This is Chile.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Chile?
items.explain: The capital of Chile is Santiago.
This is Peru.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Peru?
items.explain: The capital of Peru is Lima.
items.hook: Cusco was the old Inca capital; Lima, on the coast, is Peru’s capital today.
items.example: Machu Picchu, the Inca city in the clouds, is near Cusco.

items.explain: This is Colombia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Colombia?
items.explain: The capital of Colombia is Bogotá.
This is Venezuela.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Venezuela?
items.explain: The capital of Venezuela is Caracas.
This is Cuba.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Cuba?
items.explain: The capital of Cuba is Havana.
This is Egypt.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Egypt?
items.explain: The capital of Egypt is Cairo.
items.example: Cairo stands on the Nile, close to the pyramids of Giza.

items.explain: This is Nigeria.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Nigeria?
items.explain: The capital of Nigeria is Abuja. Abuja, not Lagos, which is the biggest city.
items.learn: The capital of **Nigeria** is **Abuja**. Abuja, not Lagos, which is the biggest city.
items.hook: Abuja was built in the middle of Nigeria and became the capital in 1991; Lagos, on the coast, is bigger.

items.explain: This is Kenya.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Kenya?
items.explain: The capital of Kenya is Nairobi.
items.hook: Nairobi comes from the Maasai words for “cool water”.

items.explain: This is Ethiopia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Ethiopia?
items.explain: The capital of Ethiopia is Addis Ababa.
items.hook: Addis Ababa means “new flower” in Amharic.

items.explain: This is Morocco.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Morocco?
items.explain: The capital of Morocco is Rabat. Rabat, not Casablanca or Marrakesh.
items.learn: The capital of **Morocco** is **Rabat**. Rabat, not Casablanca or Marrakesh.

items.explain: This is Ghana.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Ghana?
items.explain: The capital of Ghana is Accra.
This is the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

items.prompt: What is the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo?
items.explain: The capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is Kinshasa.
items.learn: The capital of **the Democratic Republic of the Congo** is **Kinshasa**.
items.hook: Kinshasa faces Brazzaville, capital of the other Congo, across the Congo River.

items.explain: This is South Africa.

items.prompt: What is the capital of South Africa?
items.explain: The capital of South Africa is Pretoria. South Africa has three capitals: Pretoria (government), Cape Town (parliament) and Bloemfontein (courts).
items.learn: The capital of **South Africa** is **Pretoria**. South Africa has three capitals: Pretoria (government), Cape Town (parliament) and Bloemfontein (courts).

items.explain: This is China.

items.prompt: What is the capital of China?
items.explain: The capital of China is Beijing.
items.hook: Beijing means “northern capital”.

items.explain: This is India.

items.prompt: What is the capital of India?
items.explain: The capital of India is New Delhi.
items.hook: New Delhi is the new part of Delhi, built by the British and opened in 1931.

items.explain: This is Japan.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Japan?
items.explain: The capital of Japan is Tokyo.
items.hook: Tokyo means “eastern capital”; Kyoto was the old capital for over 1,000 years.

items.explain: This is South Korea.

items.prompt: What is the capital of South Korea?
items.explain: The capital of South Korea is Seoul.
items.hook: Seoul is South Korea’s capital; Pyongyang is North Korea’s.

items.explain: This is Pakistan.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Pakistan?
items.explain: The capital of Pakistan is Islamabad. Islamabad, not Karachi.
items.learn: The capital of **Pakistan** is **Islamabad**. Islamabad, not Karachi.
items.hook: Islamabad was built in the 1960s as a brand-new capital; Karachi, on the coast, is much bigger.

items.explain: This is Bangladesh.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Bangladesh?
items.explain: The capital of Bangladesh is Dhaka.
This is Saudi Arabia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Saudi Arabia?
items.explain: The capital of Saudi Arabia is Riyadh.
items.hook: Mecca is the holy city, but Riyadh is the capital.

items.explain: This is Turkey.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Turkey?
items.explain: The capital of Turkey is Ankara. Ankara, not Istanbul.
items.learn: The capital of **Turkey** is **Ankara**. Ankara, not Istanbul.
items.hook: Istanbul was the old Ottoman capital; Atatürk made Ankara the capital in 1923.

items.explain: This is Iran.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Iran?
items.explain: The capital of Iran is Tehran.
This is Vietnam.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Vietnam?
items.explain: The capital of Vietnam is Hanoi.
items.hook: Hanoi in the north is the capital; Ho Chi Minh City (once Saigon), in the south, is bigger.

items.explain: This is Thailand.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Thailand?
items.explain: The capital of Thailand is Bangkok.
This is Australia.

items.prompt: What is the capital of Australia?
items.explain: The capital of Australia is Canberra. Canberra, not Sydney: it was built as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.
items.learn: The capital of **Australia** is **Canberra**. Canberra, not Sydney: it was built as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.
items.example: Canberra was designed from scratch by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin.

items.explain: This is New Zealand.

items.prompt: What is the capital of New Zealand?
items.explain: The capital of New Zealand is Wellington. Wellington, not Auckland.
items.learn: The capital of **New Zealand** is **Wellington**. Wellington, not Auckland.
items.hook: Wellington is named after the Duke of Wellington, who won the Battle of Waterloo.
